title: Carmel, again
tomorrow: at a busy tamale sale, who should get served first?

cards: Some friendships run on long voice memos. Others are two people on a couch, saying nothing, completely at ease. Both are real friendship.

Prayer has both kinds too, and someone who prays for years may meet both. And inside Carmel, the order of Teresa of Ávila and John of the Cross, the two kinds have each had a champion. So: words or silence?
Here are the two cases, each in its own voice.

teach.b: Teresa speaks first. In her Life, she describes prayer as an intimate sharing between friends: taking time, often, to be alone with the one who you know loves you.

She liked to picture Christ beside her, his face, his words, his suffering. And she pushed back on teachers who told people to set aside every image, even of Christ's humanity, in order to rise higher.
For her, that was leaving the friend behind. On this view, prayer needs a face and a conversation. John of the Cross answers.
In the Ascent of Mount Carmel, he says that a time comes when meditating with thoughts and pictures dries up, and that this can be a good sign.

Then the soul should learn to stay with God in loving attention, quietly, without working at images. Forcing words then, he says, only gets in the way. On this view, love grows past words into stillness.
The psalm says it in the Douay-Rheims Bible: "Be still and see that I am God." Here's the one to tell a friend: Teresa and John weren't rivals.
They worked together to renew Carmel, and she called him her little Seneca. They disagree about when to set the pictures down.
They agree on the heart of it: prayer is love, paying attention to God.

how: Carmelite friars and nuns spend set times each day in silent mental prayer; many Catholics learn prayer from Teresa of Ávila's Life and Interior Castle and from John of the Cross.

o: a city in Italy known for its pilgrims
an order where prayer is loving attention
a hymn sung on Easter morning at dawn

games.q: two ways in Carmel — tap the pairs.
p: be still and see that I am God

s: Teresa taught that the highest prayer leaves even Christ's humanity behind
she pushed back on that: for her, setting aside Christ's humanity was leaving the friend behind.
John of the Cross said dry meditation can be a good sign
a sign that it may be time to rest in loving attention.
Teresa and John were rivals with opposite teachings
they worked together to renew Carmel; they differ on when to set the pictures down.

games.q: you love praying with words and imagining Christ beside you. your friend says real prayer is silent. you side with Teresa. what's your friend's best case?
o: John of the Cross: when meditation dries up, rest in loving attention.
words are only for beginners, so they never count as real prayer.
silence is easier, and prayer should take as little effort as possible.
games.why: her best case is in the Ascent of Mount Carmel. yours is in Teresa's Life. both are Carmelite, and both call prayer love paying attention to God.

practice: Close your eyes and stay still. Let any words or pictures come and go without chasing them, and simply rest your attention on God, or on the quiet itself if that's where you are.
When your mind wanders, return gently, the way you'd turn back to a friend on the couch.

wordCard.voice: Carmel. The order of Teresa and John, named for a mountain, where prayer is loving attention.

orig.note: Spanish, written in Latin letters: loving attention. John of the Cross's phrase for quiet prayer.

carryVoice: Hold onto this: attention, with words like Teresa or without them like John, given in love. Good night.
